unit.title: Season Now
unit.summary: This week in pickleball: current events, draws, rankings, standings, news and seasonal changes. Lesson templates stay evergreen; live cards supply the dates, names and numbers.

lessons.title: This week in pickleball
lessons.objective: Know what's on this week and why it matters.

payload.prompt: Why do pro pickleball fans check the schedule every week?

options.text: To find out which tours have events and who's playing.
Because the schedule never changes.
To see which paddles are approved.
To read last year's results.

explanation.correct: Schedules show what's happening this week across the tours and help you follow the action.
explanation.incorrect: The schedule tells you which events are on and which players are competing. It changes every week, and it is not about paddles or old results.
explanation.sayThisLine: Events change week to week. That's why the schedule matters.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Huge week for pickleball. My favorite is playing and there's a team event on too.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Multiple things she cares about are happening at the same time.
She only cares about one player.
The weather will be big.
She's tired of pickleball.

payload.translation: When several events or favorite players are competing at once, it's a big week to follow.

followUps.line: Which one are you most excited to watch?
followUps.why: Invites her to choose and share what she cares about.
Turns a big week into time with her.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Fans track schedules to catch favorite players and events. You can just ask what she is watching.

payload.prompt: This week's schedule tells you everything you need to know about pickleball right now. True?

choices.label: No, rankings and news matter too

explanation.correct: The schedule shows what's happening, but rankings, news and standings add the meaning.
explanation.incorrect: Schedules matter, but context (who's hot, rule changes, standings) is what makes them interesting.
explanation.sayThisLine: The schedule tells you what. Rankings and news tell you why it matters.

payload.prompt: She's streaming her favorite pro tonight. What should you do?

situation.narrative: She is excited about a match that is on this week.

facts.label: What she said
facts.value: Going to stream my favorite's match tonight.

options.label: Ask to watch it with her
options.consequence: Perfect. You show interest and get to learn by watching together.
considerations: It is an easy way to follow along

options.label: Say 'have fun' and leave it
options.consequence: Kind, but you miss a chance to engage with what she loves.

payload.expertNote: Being curious about who is playing and when creates natural conversation.

payload.prompt: Complete the following-the-sport sentence.
payload.template: To know what's on, check the {{source}}, and to know why it matters, read the {{context}}.

explanation.correct: The schedule says what is on, and news and rankings explain why it matters.
explanation.incorrect: Use the schedule for what is on, and the news and rankings for the story behind it.
explanation.sayThisLine: The schedule is the what. The news is the why.

lessons.title: Read the draw
lessons.objective: Follow the current event's bracket and seeding.

payload.prompt: What does reading a draw tell you?

options.text: Who plays whom and in what order; top seeds are placed to meet late.
How much money the winner gets.
Which paddle brand most pros use.
The weather forecast for the tournament.

explanation.correct: A draw shows the bracket, the seeding and the matchup pairings for the event.
explanation.incorrect: Reading a draw tells you the structure: who faces whom and when.
explanation.sayThisLine: The draw shows the bracket. Top seeds are kept apart until late.

payload.prompt: Tap where seeds 1 and 2 start in this eight-slot bracket.

diagram.alt: Eight-slot single-elimination bracket drawn left to right. The eight first-round slots run top to bottom down the left edge.

explanation.correct: The top two seeds start at opposite ends of the bracket, so they cannot meet until the final.
explanation.incorrect: Seeds 1 and 2 are placed at opposite ends, the very top and very bottom slots, which keeps them apart until the final. The middle slots go to the next seeds.
explanation.sayThisLine: Seeds 1 and 2 are on opposite ends, so they'd only meet in the final.

payload.prompt: The draw is released before the tournament starts. True?

explanation.correct: Draws are published before the event so players can plan and fans can preview the matchups.
explanation.incorrect: The draw comes out beforehand so fans can follow the storylines and players know their path.
explanation.sayThisLine: The draw drops before the event. That's when the bracket talk starts.

payload.prompt: Match draw and bracket terms.

pairs.definition: A player's seeding rank (1, 2, 3, etc.) based on ranking; top seeds get favorable draw placement.
The published bracket showing who plays whom and the match order.
A free pass to the next round when a bracket is not full; top seeds often get them.

explanation.summary: A seed is a rank, the draw is the bracket, and a bye skips a round.
explanation.sayThisLine: Top seeds get byes and easier early draws.

payload.prompt: Complete the draw statement.
payload.template: A {{seed}} seed is placed in the draw so they avoid other top players {{when}}.

explanation.correct: Top seeds are placed to avoid each other until the later rounds, so the biggest matches come late.
explanation.incorrect: Seeding protects the top players from meeting early. Low seeds are the ones who can draw a top seed in the first round.
explanation.sayThisLine: Top seeds are kept apart so the big matches come late.

lessons.title: Rankings movers
lessons.objective: Interpret who moved in the world rankings and why.

payload.prompt: What causes a player's world ranking to jump up?

options.text: Strong results and the ranking points they earn.
Being popular on social media.
Having the best paddle.
Playing the most matches.

explanation.correct: Tournament results and the points they earn are what move a player's ranking.
explanation.incorrect: Rankings move because of results and points, not popularity, equipment or sheer number of matches.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rankings move on results, not on hype.

payload.prompt: She was 12th and dropped 4 places. Where is she now?

explanation.correct: 12 plus 4 is 16. Dropping means the ranking number gets bigger, so she is now 16th.
explanation.incorrect: A drop moves her away from number one, so the number goes up: 12 plus 4 is 16th. Moving up would make the number smaller.
explanation.sayThisLine: She slipped from 12th to 16th.

payload.prompt: A big ranking jump always means the player won the event. True?

choices.label: No, strong results can do it too

explanation.correct: Right. A deep run or several strong results can earn enough points for a jump without a title.
explanation.incorrect: Points come from results across events, so a deep run or a string of good weeks can move a player a long way without winning.
explanation.sayThisLine: Did she win it, or was it a bunch of strong weeks?

payload.prompt: Her favorite player jumped from 23rd to 8th. What usually drives that?

situation.narrative: She sends you a screenshot of the rankings, and the movement is big.

facts.label: Your question
facts.value: What usually drives a move like that?

options.label: Strong recent results earned her more ranking points
options.consequence: Right. A big climb usually comes from strong results and the points that come with them.
considerations: Upward moves come from earned points

options.label: She took a break and relaxed
options.consequence: No. A break does not earn points. A jump like this comes from strong results.
considerations: A break does not help a ranking

payload.expertNote: Upward movement usually signals strong recent results. Ask which event she thinks caused it.

payload.prompt: Complete the ranking statement.
payload.template: When a player's ranking jumps, it usually means they had {{action}} and earned {{what}}.

explanation.correct: Strong results earn ranking points, and points move the ranking up.
explanation.incorrect: Ranking jumps come from results and the points they earn, not from time off or gear.
explanation.sayThisLine: A jump in the rankings means strong results. Ask her about the event.

lessons.title: MLP standings
lessons.objective: Read the current MLP table and playoff picture.

payload.prompt: What do MLP standings show you?

options.text: How each team is doing and where they sit in the playoff race.
How many individual players are on each team.
Which paddle brand each team uses.
The age of each team's players.

explanation.correct: Standings rank the teams by their results and show who is in playoff position.
explanation.incorrect: MLP standings rank teams by results and show who is in or out of the playoff picture, not rosters, brands or ages.
explanation.sayThisLine: The standings tell you where her team stands in the race.

payload.title: Standings watch
payload.setting: Sam's team is in a playoff race.

exchanges.theirMessage: We're right on the playoff bubble, two wins out of a spot. Still in it!

replies.text: Two wins back with how many events left?
replies.theirResponse: Four left. We can make it up.
replies.coachNote: You understood the standings and asked a practical question.

replies.theirResponse: Yeah, barely. Hoping we can climb.
replies.coachNote: Kind but general. Ask about the path to the playoffs.

replies.text: You'll never make the playoffs from there.
replies.coachNote: You discouraged her. With events left, the race is still open.

payload.closingNote: In MLP, teams climb the standings by winning matches. Being a couple of wins back with events left is still very much in play.

payload.prompt: A winning record guarantees a playoff spot. True?

choices.label: No, position and matches left matter

explanation.correct: Right. Playoff spots go to teams who finish high enough in the standings, so a record only helps relative to the other teams.
explanation.incorrect: A good record helps, but where you sit relative to the playoff line and how many matches remain decide who gets in.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's not just the record. It's where they sit against the playoff line.

payload.prompt: Order the MLP season arc.

items.text: Teams climb and drop in the standings

explanation.sayThisLine: Season opens, standings move, playoffs decide the champion.
explanation.correct: MLP seasons flow from the regular season, through the standings race, to the playoffs and a final champion.
explanation.incorrect: The regular season builds the standings, the standings set the playoff field, and the playoffs lead to the champion.

payload.prompt: Complete the standings statement.
payload.template: In MLP, the standings change {{frequency}} because {{reason}}.

options: wins and losses move teams up and down
gaps.correct: wins and losses move teams up and down

explanation.correct: Standings update as match results come in, because wins and losses move teams up and down.
explanation.incorrect: Standings are not frozen. They change whenever results come in, as wins and losses reshuffle the teams.
explanation.sayThisLine: Every result reshuffles the standings.

lessons.title: The news explainer
lessons.objective: Understand why a pickleball headline is a big deal.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Did you see the paddle news? I'm worried mine won't be legal anymore.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: A new rule or test could mean some paddles are no longer approved for sanctioned play.
She's going to spin a paddle and fail a fitness test.
All paddles are being destroyed.
She's being dramatic about nothing.

payload.translation: Equipment rules change. When they do, some gear may have to be re-checked or may not meet the new standard.

followUps.line: Are you thinking about a backup paddle just in case?
followUps.why: A practical question that shows you listened.

followUps.line: What did the news actually say about your model?
followUps.why: Invites her to explain instead of you guessing.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rule and equipment changes are normal and create gear-talk opportunities. Ask what she read.

payload.prompt: Why do pickleball fans care about rule changes?

options.text: Rules change the game they play or watch and affect strategy.
Rule changes always make the game easier.
Rules don't matter; people just talk about them.
Rules only apply to the pros.

explanation.correct: Rule changes affect how the game is played and which strategies work.
explanation.incorrect: New rules matter because they reshape how people play and watch. They are not always easier, and they reach players at every level.
explanation.sayThisLine: A rule change is a change to the game she loves. That's why people care.

payload.prompt: Equipment news like paddle approvals only matters to pros. True?

choices.label: No, it reaches everyday players too

explanation.correct: Right. Anyone entering sanctioned events needs approved gear, and everyday players buy the same paddles the news is about.
explanation.incorrect: Approved-gear rules apply to sanctioned events at every level, and rec players buy the same paddles. Casual park games rarely check, but the news still touches them.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rule news isn't just for the pros. It affects what we buy.

payload.prompt: She mentions a rule change you don't understand. What do you do?

situation.narrative: Rule talk can be confusing if you're new.

facts.label: What she said
facts.value: Something about the serve rules got tighter.

options.label: Ask her to explain what tightened
options.consequence: Perfect. She gets to teach you and feels heard.

options.label: Nod and change the subject
options.consequence: Safe, but you miss learning and showing interest.

payload.expertNote: Asking about rule changes is a natural way to learn and show interest.

payload.prompt: Pick the best move when she mentions rule news.
payload.template: When she mentions a rule change, {{move}} and let her {{role}}.

explanation.correct: Asking what changed and letting her explain shows real interest and keeps you honest.
explanation.incorrect: Pretending to know is easy to spot. Ask what changed and let her explain it in her own words.
explanation.sayThisLine: I haven't read that one. What changed?

lessons.title: New season primer
lessons.objective: Reset for a new season or major rulebook update.

payload.prompt: Why do fans talk about a 'new season' at different times of year?

options.text: Different tours run on different calendars, so each starts its year at its own time.
Every tour starts on the same day.
Pickleball is only played in summer.
New seasons only begin when a rule changes.

explanation.correct: Each tour sets its own calendar, so a new season can be starting in one part of the sport while another is wrapping up. The live card shows the current dates.
explanation.incorrect: Tours do not share one calendar, and pickleball is played year-round. The live card shows when each season starts.
explanation.sayThisLine: Which tour's season are we talking about? They don't all start together.

payload.prompt: Order a five-minute catch-up for a new season.

items.text: Check the calendar for what is on
Pick one storyline to ask her about

explanation.sayThisLine: Calendar, rules, rankings, then one good question.
explanation.correct: Start with what is on, add what changed, see who is moving, and finish with one storyline to ask her about.
explanation.incorrect: Work from the broad picture down: what is on, what changed, who is moving, then one storyline to ask about.

payload.prompt: A new season means you have to relearn the whole game. True?

choices.label: No, most of the game stays the same

explanation.correct: Right. The core game carries over, and the changes are usually small clarifications and a few new storylines.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen, the serve and the scoring carry over from season to season. New seasons bring a few tweaks and fresh storylines, not a new game.
explanation.sayThisLine: Same game, new season. Just a few tweaks to catch up on.

payload.prompt: The new rulebook is out and she's buzzing about one change. Your move?

situation.narrative: A fresh rulebook edition just arrived, and she has opinions.

facts.label: What happened
facts.value: A new rulebook edition is out

options.label: Ask which change she's excited or annoyed about
options.consequence: She launches into it. You learn what matters to her, and she gets to be the expert.

options.label: Promise to read the whole rulebook tonight
options.consequence: Sweet, but it is a lot, and it skips the easier win of just asking her.

options.label: Say the rules never really change
options.consequence: They do change, and she just told you about one. It makes you sound like you were not listening.
considerations: A new edition comes out each year

payload.expertNote: A new rulebook edition is a built-in conversation starter. Ask which change she cares about and listen.

payload.prompt: Complete the new-season statement.
payload.template: A new-season primer covers the {{first}}, the latest rankings and any {{last}} changes.

explanation.correct: A primer covers the calendar, where the rankings stand, and any rule changes.
explanation.incorrect: New-season catch-ups focus on the calendar, the rankings and rule changes, not prices or lighting.
explanation.sayThisLine: New season: check the calendar, the rankings and the rule changes.
